present.name: Verb endings with ich, du, wir and the rest
present.about: Most verbs end in -e with ich, -st with du, -t with er, sie, es or ihr, and -en with wir, sie or Sie; if the part before -en ends in s, ß, x or z, du takes only -t: ich arbeite, du arbeitest, wir arbeiten, du heißt.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

present.short: The verb's ending says who: ich trinke, du trinkst, er trinkt, wir trinken (I drink, you drink, he drinks, we drink).

v2.name: Verb second
v2.about: In a main clause the verb comes second. Start with a time word, and the subject moves after the verb: Morgen fahren wir (tomorrow go we).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

v2.short: In a main clause the verb comes second, even after a time or a place: Hier ist mein Schlüssel (here is my key).

question.name: Questions: verb first or after the question word
question.about: In a yes-or-no question the verb comes first; after a question word, it comes next: Wo wohnst du (where live you).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

question.short: A yes-or-no question starts with the verb: Bist du fertig? (are you ready?) After a question word, the verb comes next: Wo ist das Auto?

gender.name: der, die, das
gender.about: Every noun is masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das), and ein, kein, mein and the rest match it: der Bahnhof, die Bank, das Haus.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gender.short: Every noun is a der, die or das word, and ein, mein and the rest match it: der Tisch, die Milch, das Handy.

accusative.name: den for a masculine object
accusative.about: When a masculine noun is the object of the verb, der becomes den and ein becomes einen: Ich habe den Zug verpasst (I have the train missed).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

accusative.short: A der word as the object takes den and einen: Ich habe den Schlüssel, Ich trinke einen Kaffee (I have the key, I'm having a coffee).

dative.name: dem after mit, in, auf …
dative.about: After mit, zu, von, bei, and in or auf for where something is, der and das become dem, a feminine die becomes der, and a plural die becomes den, with the noun usually adding -n: mit dem Bus (with the bus), mit den Kindern (with the children).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Short name made to cover der and den too in revision 6 (the director, 2026-11-09).

dative.short: After auf, in or mit, for where something is or what it's with, der and das become dem and die becomes der: auf dem Tisch, in der Tasche.

nicht.name: Where nicht goes
nicht.about: nicht usually comes after the object and time words, near the end, but before a place word, an adjective or a verb at the end: Ich kenne ihn nicht (I know him not).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

nicht.short: nicht comes after the object, near the end, but before ready, here or home: Ich habe das Buch nicht, Ich bin nicht fertig.

kein.name: kein: no, not a
kein.about: Before a noun, German says kein (no) where English says not a or not any: Ich habe kein Auto (I have no car).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

kein.short: Before a noun, German says kein where English says not a or not any: Ich habe kein Auto (I have no car).

perfect.name: Past with haben: second verb last
perfect.about: To talk about the past with haben, put the second verb in its past form at the end: Ich habe ein Buch gelesen (I have a book read).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

perfect.short: Past with haben: the second verb, in its past form, goes to the end: Ich habe ein Buch gelesen (I have a book read).

sein-perfect.name: Past with sein
sein-perfect.about: Verbs of going from place to place, and a few more, take sein instead of haben: Wir sind nach Hamburg gefahren (we are to Hamburg traveled).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

sein-perfect.short: Verbs of going somewhere take sein instead of haben: Wir sind nach Hause gegangen (we are home gone).

modal.name: können, müssen, wollen, möchten: second verb last
modal.about: With können, müssen, wollen or möchten, the second verb goes to the end, with no word for to: Ich will heute schwimmen (I want today swim).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

modal.short: After können, müssen or wollen, the second verb goes to the end, with no word for to: Ich will Kaffee trinken (I want coffee drink).

separable.name: Separable verbs
separable.about: Verbs like aufstehen split: the verb comes second and the little word (auf) goes to the end: Ich stehe um sieben auf (I stand at seven up).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

separable.short: Verbs like aufstehen split: the verb comes second and the little word goes to the end: Ich stehe um sieben auf (I stand at seven up).

dass.name: dass: verb to the end
dass.about: After dass (that), the verb goes to the end of its clause: Ich glaube, dass sie heute arbeitet (I believe that she today works).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

dass.short: After dass (that), the verb goes to the end of its clause: Ich glaube, dass sie heute arbeitet (I believe that she today works).

weil.name: weil: because, verb last
weil.about: After weil (because), the verb goes to the end of its clause too: weil ich müde bin (because I tired am).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

weil.short: After weil (because), the verb goes to the end too: weil ich müde bin (because I tired am).

es-gibt.name: es gibt: there is or there are
es-gibt.about: es gibt introduces existence or availability and takes an accusative object: Hier gibt es ein Sofa.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2. Changed in revision 5. Short name made to cover there are too in revision 6 (the director, 2026-11-09).

es-gibt.chip: es gibt: there is or are
es-gibt.short: Hier gibt es ein Sofa means there is a sofa here. The thing introduced is an accusative object.

gern.name: gern: liking to do
gern.about: To say you like doing something, put gern (gladly) after the verb: Ich trinke gern Kaffee (I drink gladly coffee).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gern.short: To say you like doing something, put gern after the verb: Ich trinke gern Kaffee (I drink gladly coffee: I like drinking coffee).

time-place.name: Time before place
time-place.about: German usually puts the time before the place: Ich fahre morgen nach München (I go tomorrow to Munich), where English often puts the time last.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

time-place.short: German puts the time before the place: Ich fahre morgen nach München (I go tomorrow to Munich).

destination.name: Going somewhere: nach, zu, in
destination.about: Use nach with cities and most countries, zu with people and places such as work, and in with places you go into: nach München, zur Arbeit, ins Kino.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

destination.short: Going somewhere: nach for cities and home (nach Hause), zu for people and work, in for places you go into: ins Kino.

possessive.name: mein, dein: my and your
possessive.about: mein (my) and dein (your, to someone you say du to) go before a der or das word, meine and deine before a die word: mein Schlüssel, mein Handy, meine Tasche. Like ein, they change with the noun's role: meinen, meinem, meiner.

source.note: Added with the German lessons, open to correction. Short name made to cover dein too in revision 6 (the director, 2026-11-09).

possessive.short: mein and dein go before a der or das word, meine and deine before a die word: mein Schlüssel, meine Tasche (my key, my bag).

demonstrative.name: dieser: this; das: that
demonstrative.about: dieser (this) matches its noun the way der, die and das do: dieser Tisch, diese Tasche, dieses Buch. On its own, das points at a thing: Das ist mein Haus (that is my house).

source.note: Added with the German lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.short: dieses goes with a das word and diese with a die word, for this: dieses Buch, diese Tasche. On its own, das is that: Das ist mein Haus.

formal-sie.name: Sie: polite you
formal-sie.about: Sie, always with a capital S, is the polite you, for someone you don't know well, to one person or more. Its verb is the same as with wir: Wissen Sie, wo das ist? (know you where that is?), Das ist für Sie (that is for you).

source.note: Added with the German lessons, open to correction.

formal-sie.short: Sie, with a capital S, is the polite you, to one person or more; its verb is the same as with wir: Wissen Sie? Wollen Sie einen Kaffee?

adjective-endings.name: Adjectives before nouns
adjective-endings.about: An adjective before a noun takes an ending that depends on gender, number, case and any determiner. Compare diese rote Karte, ein lustiges Buch and schwarze Sachen. After ist, a description such as rot has no adjective ending.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3. Changed in revision 7.

adjective-endings.short: Before a noun: diese rote Karte, ein lustiges Buch, schwarze Sachen. As a description after ist: Die Karte ist rot.

question-word.name: Asking with a question word
question-word.about: In a direct question, wo asks where, was asks what, and wie asks how. In an ordinary question, the question word or phrase comes first, then the finite verb.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

question-word.short: A question word says what you ask: Wie kann ich helfen? (How can I help?).

verb-case.name: Learn the case with the verb
verb-case.about: helfen takes a dative object: Ich helfe meinem Freund. A direct object of haben takes the accusative: Ich habe den Schlüssel.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

verb-case.short: helfen takes the dative: Ich helfe meinem Freund (I'm helping my friend).

time-telling.name: Saying at what time
time-telling.about: um gives the time of an event. Use the hour with Uhr, or halb toward the coming hour, or Viertel nach and Viertel vor for quarter hours.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3. Short name made to cover other hours too in revision 6 (the director, 2026-11-09). Changed in revision 7.

time-telling.short: um zwei Uhr means at two o'clock. halb drei is half past two; Viertel nach zwei is a quarter past two, and Viertel vor drei is a quarter to three.

purpose.name: Purpose: um … zu and damit
purpose.about: um … zu expresses purpose with a shared understood subject. damit introduces a finite purpose clause with its own subject, which may differ from the main clause subject.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3. Changed in revision 6.

purpose.short: Use um … zu for a purpose with the same understood subject; damit + subject and a final finite verb can also introduce a different subject.

object-pronouns.name: Pronouns after verbs and prepositions
object-pronouns.about: The verb or preposition determines a pronoun's case. After bei, du becomes the dative dir: bei dir.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

object-pronouns.short: After bei, du becomes dir: Ich bin bei dir (I'm with you).

imperative.name: Requests and commands
imperative.about: For a request to du, use a command form, usually without du: Ruf deinen Vater an. A polite request keeps Sie: Rufen Sie den Arzt an, bitte.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

imperative.short: Ruf … an addresses du; Rufen Sie … an is polite. bitte can soften either request.

particles.name: Small words that shape the tone
particles.about: In these requests, mal makes the request sound casual and less abrupt. It is not a fixed translation of a particular English word.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3.

particles.short: mal can soften a request: Ruf meine Mutter mal an (Give my mother a call).

indirect-question.name: A question inside a sentence
indirect-question.about: A question embedded inside another sentence uses a question word such as was, or ob for whether. Its finite verb normally goes last: was ich machen muss; ob jeder dabei ist.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3. Changed in revision 7.

indirect-question.short: Use a question word for what is asked, or ob for whether: Kontrolliere, ob jeder dabei ist. The embedded finite verb goes last.

zu-infinitive.name: An infinitive with zu
zu-infinitive.about: Use zu with infinitives after expressions such as versuchen, vergessen, schwierig or Zeit haben. Separable verbs put zu inside: anzurufen. A modal takes a bare infinitive.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 3. Changed in revision 6.

zu-infinitive.short: viel zu tun means a lot to do. Other expressions also take zu with an infinitive.

coordination.name: Joining clauses and actions
coordination.about: und, aber and oder join words, phrases or clauses; denn joins a reason with main-clause order. und can join two finite verbs with one shared subject: Ich sitze und lese.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 6.

coordination.short: und joins actions or clauses. denn joins a reason without changing main-clause verb order.

quantity-pronouns.name: An amount without repeating the noun
quantity-pronouns.about: genug and ein bisschen can stand on their own when the food or drink is understood: Ich habe genug. Nimmst du auch ein bisschen?

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4.

quantity-pronouns.short: You can leave an understood noun out after genug or ein bisschen: Ich habe genug (I have enough).

two-way-prepositions.name: A location or a destination
two-way-prepositions.about: With the place prepositions in, an and auf, a location uses dative and a destination or new position uses accusative: auf dem Tisch, but auf den Tisch. Movement alone does not decide the case.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4.

two-way-prepositions.short: A location: Das Foto steht auf dem Tisch. A new position: Ich stelle das Foto auf den Tisch.

temporal-clauses.name: Until, when, while and before
temporal-clauses.about: bis gives an endpoint; wenn introduces a condition or repeated or future occasion; als places an event on a single past occasion or in a past period; während connects simultaneous events, and bevor places one event before another. These clauses end with their finite verb.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

temporal-clauses.short: A time clause ends with its finite verb. Choose the joining word for the intended time relation.

plural.name: More than one book
plural.about: Learn a noun with its plural. Buch becomes Bücher; the dative plural is Büchern: in den Büchern. Plural articles do not depend on the singular gender.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4.

plural.short: One: das Buch. More than one: die Bücher. After in for a location: in den Büchern.

reflexive.name: Myself and yourself with setzen
reflexive.about: A reflexive pronoun refers back to the subject. The construction determines its case: mich and dich in sitting down, sich in Sie hat sich gesehen, and dative sich after mit in Er redet mit sich selbst.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 7.

reflexive.short: mich refers back to ich, dich to du, and sich can refer back to er or sie. Compare Sie hat sich gesehen and Er redet mit sich selbst.

comparative.name: Bigger, better, more and rather
comparative.about: Many comparative forms add -er, sometimes with an umlaut: groß → größer. als introduces the other side of an unequal comparison. Irregular forms include besser, mehr and lieber.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 6.

comparative.short: Use größer or kleiner to compare sizes, with als for than. gut becomes besser, viel becomes mehr and gern becomes lieber.

nominal-infinitive.name: An activity as a noun
nominal-infinitive.about: An infinitive used as a noun names an activity. The noun is neuter and capitalized: das Fahren. Compare the verb fahren in Ich will fahren lernen with the noun in Das Fahren ist nicht so schwierig.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4.

nominal-infinitive.short: The activity is a noun: das Fahren. Write it with a capital and use das; the verb fahren stays lowercase.

weak-nouns.name: Herr becomes Herrn
weak-nouns.about: Some masculine nouns change outside nominative singular: der Herr, den Herrn; der Präsident, den Präsidenten and des Präsidenten. Learn the pattern with each noun; it is not a rule for every masculine noun.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 7.

weak-nouns.short: The noun changes too: der Herr becomes den Herrn; der Präsident becomes den Präsidenten. The genitive is des Präsidenten, without -s.

ordinal.name: First: erste and ersten
ordinal.about: erste and zweite give positions in a sequence. They take adjective endings: der zweite Gast, den zweiten Gast and mit dem zweiten Gast. The ending depends on the whole noun phrase.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 4. Changed in revision 7.

ordinal.short: Use erste for first and zweite for second; the ending changes with the phrase: der zweite Gast, mit dem zweiten Gast.

subject-pronouns.name: Who does it: subject pronouns
subject-pronouns.about: A subject pronoun can carry a contrast or stand without a repeated verb. Lowercase sie can mean she or they; the verb distinguishes sie ist from sie sind. Mid-sentence, capitalized Sie marks polite you. Sentence-initial capitalization does not distinguish these readings.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5.

subject-pronouns.short: Ihr geht, wir nicht: you guys are going, we are not. sie ist means she is; sie sind means they are. Mid-sentence Sie is polite you.

clause-first.name: A whole clause in first place
clause-first.about: A subordinate clause can fill the first position of a statement. Its own finite verb goes last; the main finite verb then follows the comma before the main subject. A command can follow too: Wenn du Zeit hast, schick mir das Foto.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5.

clause-first.short: Wenn du fertig bist, kannst du mich anrufen: bist ends the opening clause, and kannst comes before du in the main clause.

past.name: Common past forms
past.about: war, hatte and past modal forms describe past states, obligations and abilities. These forms are common in conversation and agree with their subject. The haben forms shown now include hatte, hattest and hatten.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

past.short: war, hatte, musste and konnte describe past states, obligations or abilities. The form changes with its subject.

conditional.name: Wishes, advice and imagined situations
conditional.about: würde with an infinitive and forms such as hätte, wäre and könnte express wishes or imagined situations. hätte or wäre with a participle can describe an unreal past. sollte can express what should happen.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

conditional.short: würde, hätte, wäre and könnte describe imagined situations; sollte can express advice or what should happen.

future.name: Plans and predictions
future.about: The present with a future time expression often describes a plan. A form of werden with a final infinitive can also express a future action or prediction.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5. Short name made to cover predictions with werden too in revision 6 (the director, 2026-11-09).

future.short: Ich rufe morgen an uses the present for a plan. Ich werde dich morgen anrufen uses werden and an infinitive.

genitive.name: Whose, of and during
genitive.about: The genitive expresses ownership and relationships, and follows während in careful standard usage: während des Films. Masculine and neuter singular nouns normally take des and -(e)s; feminine nouns take der.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

genitive.short: wessen asks whose; des Films means of the movie. während des Films means during the movie.

modal-perfect.name: Two infinitives in the perfect
modal-perfect.about: With sehen, lassen or a modal followed by another infinitive, these perfect constructions use haben and two infinitives: hat gehen müssen. In a subordinate modal group, haben precedes both infinitives.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

modal-perfect.short: Er hat gehen müssen: haben plus the action infinitive and müssen. After dass, the modal group is dass er hat gehen müssen.

seit-present.name: Still true since then
seit-present.about: seit with a starting point or time span and a present-tense verb describes a situation continuing now. A noun phrase after seit takes the dative.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5.

seit-present.short: Seit einem Monat schlafe ich wenig uses the present for something continuing now. seit takes the dative: einem Monat.

relative.name: A clause about a noun
relative.about: A relative clause adds information about a noun. Its pronoun matches that noun in gender and number but takes its case from its role in the relative clause. The finite verb goes last.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 5. Changed in revision 6.

relative.short: Der Job, den ich will, ist hier: a relative clause describes a noun and ends with its finite verb.

pronominal-adverbs.name: About it and about what
pronominal-adverbs.about: da- plus a preposition refers to things or situations; wo- plus a preposition asks about them. Insert r before a vowel: daran, woran, worüber. For people, normally use a preposition and a pronoun.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

pronominal-adverbs.short: darauf, daran and davon refer to a thing or situation; woran and worüber ask what it is. The verb helps determine the preposition.

past-perfect.name: Before another past moment
past-perfect.about: hatte or war with a past participle places an event before another past reference point. Use the past form of the same haben or sein that the verb takes in the perfect.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

past-perfect.short: Ich hatte schon gegessen; sie war schon gegangen. The event comes before a past moment in the story.

passive.name: An action or its resulting state
passive.about: werden + a past participle presents an action; sein + a participle can describe its resulting state. The past action uses wurde or ist … worden. von + dative can name the agent.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

passive.short: Das Essen wird gemacht describes the action. Die Tür ist geschlossen describes the state. Die Tür ist geschlossen worden reports the past action.

superlative.name: The biggest: superlatives
superlative.about: The superlative gives the highest degree within a comparison group. Use am -(e)sten on its own, or an adjective ending before a noun: am größten, das größte Haus.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 6.

superlative.short: Dieses Haus ist am größten and das größte Haus both identify the biggest house in the comparison.

diminutive.name: Small or affectionate: -chen and -lein
diminutive.about: The endings -chen and -lein can make a noun small or affectionate. These diminutives are neuter, often add an umlaut, and keep the same form in the plural.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 7.

diminutive.short: das Büchlein and das Bänkchen are neuter. Their plurals keep the same form: die Büchlein, die Bänkchen.
